title: Potential Effects of Nonantibiotic Emerging Contaminant Degradation on Antibiotic Resistance Genes in Effluent‐Impacted Hyporheic Zones
content:
A custom database of environmental contaminant degradation pathways and associated genes enabled integrated profiling of ARGs and ECDGs in hyporheic zone sediments. Sequence assembly and MAG reconstruction revealed their co-occurrence and potential microbial hosts, linking contaminant degradation potential to the co-selection and dissemination of antibiotic resistance.


ABSTRACT

Hyporheic zones (HZs) are hotspots of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in rivers. Nonantibiotic emerging contaminants (ECs) discharged from wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) can exert selective pressure on microbial communities and contribute to ARGs dissemination. However, the role of microbial ECs degradation in ARGs dissemination through co-selection remains poorly understood. In this study, HZs sediment samples were collected from two rivers dominated by WWTPs effluent and analyzed using metagenomic sequencing to investigate the co-selection effects of ECs on ARGs. A custom database of ECs degradation genes (ECDGs) was constructed by integrating information from EnviPath, KEGG Xenobiotics modules, and Eawag-BBD, totally covering 187 contaminants. Using this database, ECDGs associated with 78 ECs were identified, with genes associated with industrial pollutants predominating. After samples affected by a WWTP shutdown were excluded, ARGs and ECDGs were significantly correlated across both rivers and seasons (p < 0.05). Network analysis identified 11 potential ECDGs hosts that were also associated with ARGs, with Phenylobacterium being the most abundant genus. Co-localization analysis revealed 3824 contigs harboring both ARGs and ECDGs, of which 2395 were identified as plasmid-like sequences. These findings suggest widespread potential for co-resistance involving ARGs and ECDGs. In addition, a total of 4250 open reading frames (ORFs) were identified as having cross-resistance potential. Analysis of reconstructed metagenome-assembled genomes recovered complete pathways for kanamycin resistance and ibuprofen degradation that shared an ORF. These site-specific results provide genomic evidence that ECs discharged from WWTPs could promote ARGs dissemination through co-selection in HZs.
